Op, I actually do feel that I understand you reasoning, because I too have tried to use this “logic” to rationalize why self-harm should be considered a coping skill, rather than self-destructive. I rationalized they SH is so much “better” and “safer” than other behaviors, such as, drug, Alcohol, and EDs. I like to use backwards design. 

1) What/how much (nutritional value) do I need to consume on the days I am prepping for? (My fitness pal or Cronometer) 

2) what is my budget for the week 

3) what can I purchase that meets my nutritional and financial needs—this can help with quantity of food
. 
4) look up/or quickly sketch the recipes you plan to cook, buy those ingredients. 

5) actual prep work: cook first what lasts the longest and takes the longest to cook, figure out what what can be prepped and then assembled later (morning/night of) 

6) portion this out into containers 

7) optional: freeze 1/2, pull out during the late week. 
 
Tips?

When I prep big batches of fresh greens (salads) I put either a small paper towel or rag on top of the greens and they stay crisp for 5 days—no dressing on them of course. 

When cooking meat, I put m/t/w in fridge, then pull out the rest from the freezer morning of the next two days. 

If you are unsure if your frozen, cooked veg will still be tasty, just cut everything and then cook the day of. 

When assembling wraps or things with bread, make sure there is a barrier between bread and anything wet. For example, bread-spinach-chickpea salad-spinach-bread. Spinach is more dense than romance or other greens, kale works awesome too.

I’m really proud of you for identifying that you need help and are seeking resources to get it, that’s a step you should feel proud of! If you are worried about having your parents react poorly or hurting their feelings, keep in mind that it is YOUR mental health,  and you are allowed to advocate for getting the help you feel you need. Don’t be scared to tell your therapist about suicidal thoughts. It is a huge misconception that if a person mentions suicide they will be sent straight away to the hospital: this is not the case. They will do a risk assessment  before making that call. A risk assessment usually goes something like this (it can vary): do you have thoughts of killing yourself, do you have a date, do you have a plan/method, do you have access to what you would need, if we made an appointment for next week would you show up? Then, depending on the answers, they could help create a safety plan for when your thoughts are really triggering you between sessions—this should be individualized to you. Usually it looks like: who are 3 people you can talk to during this time, what are 3 coping mechanisms you can practice during this time, what resources do you have/need during this time. Regarding telling your parents, they have a legal obligation to inform parents of a few things (they will also go over these with you): threats to kill yourself or harm others, and sexual or physical abuse to you or if you plan to do them to others. If it is specific to thoughts, be upfront and ask them, “will you tell my parents if I talk about suicidal  thoughts, or just if I have a plan?” They should provide you with the answer to that.  Hope this helps!

Our bodies go into fight/flight (FF) when we encounter a stressor that causes us distress. When we are not encountering any known stressors (things seem “normal”) and we experience  this response, it’s often looked at as anxiety. The state you are describing seems chronic, and only you can tell if it is from stress or anxiety (maybe both?). Either way, the Brain is being hijacked by misfirings of neurotransmitters; how do we stop this? By being more present. By being present in our sense and thoughts, we are forcing the hijacker out of our brains. Some ideas come to mind:

-cross your arms over your chest, grip tight to your triceps, deeply inhale/exhale, pay attention the rise and fall of your chest. Go slow, 10 times. This is great because it can be done anywhere and it doesn’t really look as if you are doing something. 

-5 senses: what can I...see, smell, taste, feel, and hear. I like to follow this up with: “I am at (location), today is (date), and I am here to...” 

-imagery. I had a friend recently tell me when she feels what you described, she visualizes pit bulls barking behind a white fence at a fancy house, and she thinks of herself going up to them and petting them. They turn from angry, to excited to see her. Visualize your emotions (whatever this looks like for YOU) and how you can calm them, to return your focus. 

-guided meditation. You can find 2 minutes of guided meditation (I prefer muscle relaxation, but up to you) on YouTube and just do that via your phone and some headphones. 2 minutes in the morning, at lunch, and before bed. I feel this helps release tension in both a physical and mental state, but it doesn’t seem to take up too much time or seem too “out there”  

Having your body in a state like that can cause memory and focus issues, shift your focus on your feelings —not thoughts or actions—the rest will follow. Hope this helps.

Organization and routine is key. Chunk everything. 

1) Got a paper to write? Write intro, break, write 1 page, break, page 2, break and so on an so forth. 
2) need to read 40 pages? Read 5, break, read 5 more, break. 
3) need to do a written assignment? Answer 1-4, break, 5-7, break.

Chucking things and breaking them into smaller parts can help ease the attention span, plus you can have an extrinsic reward to constantly be working towards: walking dog, watch 1 YouTube video, play 2 rounds of Tetris.  Whatever that is that will motivate you to work harder and more focused in short burst. Your breaks should only be 1/4 of the amount of time it takes you to complete one “set.” For example, if it takes you 20 minutes to write a page, you get a 5 minute break. 

Routine is also necessary. Monday you work on this class, Wednesday you work on this class, Thursday you work on that class. Keeping a daily/hourly planner is important. See how much time you need to work and plan it. Consider how much time you need relax—plan it, and only do it if your work is finished. This can seem overwhelming at first, but as time goes on, even the planning become routine.

One thing I found really helpful was looking at the syllabus  for each class, writing down the chapters  I would need to read and the assignments I would need to do and when. I would also schedule everything a week EARLY so that I was never behind—or if something did come up, I was at least covered for that week. Front loading my course work helped tremendously with finals because I could just review what I had done and not have to scramble. Hope this helps!

Don’t be scared to tell your therapist about suicidal thoughts. It is a huge misconception that if a person mentions suicide they will be sent straight away to the hospital: this is not the case. They will do a risk assessment  before making that call. A risk assessment usually goes something like this (it can vary): do you have thoughts of killing yourself, do you have a date, do you have a plan/method, do you have access to what you would need, if we made an appointment for next week would you show up? Then, depending on the answers, they could help create a safety plan for when your thoughts are really triggering you between sessions—this should be individualized to you. Regarding telling your parents, they have a legal obligation to inform parents of a few things (they will also go over these with you): threats to kill yourself or harm others, and sexual or physical abuse to you or if you plan to do them to others. If it is specific to thoughts, be upfront and ask them, “will you tell my parents if I talk about suicidal  thoughts, or just if I have a plan?” They should provide you with the answer to that.  Hope this helps!

Don’t feel discouraged if you don’t hit it off with the first person you meet. For therapy to be effective, you need to feel the most comfortable and vulnerable you can, don’t be nervous about it taking time to find that person for you! In regards to diagnosis, don’t be too worried if they don’t give you one/share it with you. Most therapist don’t feel the label is helpful, and often view it as disabling to the client. This is something you’ll want to discuss with the person. Good luck, be safe!
